newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss ready to probe financial ties to Nazi Germany.
newsitem.headline: Swiss ready to probe financial ties to Nazi Germany.

text.p: Eight historians and a lawyer empowered to lift Swiss bank secrecy laws will meet for the first time this week to launch a sweeping probe of neutral Switzerland's controversial financial ties to Nazi Germany.

The five Swiss and four foreign experts will meet in Berne from March 5 to 8 after being hastily picked by the Swiss government in December to answer a hail of international criticism that Switzerland profited from World War Two.

The meeting takes place amid a debate among the Swiss about their past and over whether the government should pay into a Holocaust memorial fund launched last week with money from Swiss banks, accused of hoarding the savings of Holocaust victims.
On Saturday Christoph Blocher, a right-wing politician and industrialist, said the Swiss should offer neither compensation nor apologies for any alleged wrongdoing during the war.

The group of experts, known as the Bergier commission after its chairman Jean-Francois Bergier, is expected to devote its inaugural session to drafting a strategy and settling practical matters such as hiring a team of 20 or so researchers.
"The commission will try to come up with a fairly detailed strategy and plan of how to tackle our tasks in the next year or two," said Linus von Castelnur, chief of staff of the panel's secretariat.

The Bergier commission has an initial mandate of five years and plans to report to the Federal Council, or cabinet, every six months, more often if it finds pointers to lost wealth or evidence of Swiss misdeeds.

It is another major step in Swiss efforts to repair its tarnished international image after months of bitter argument with Jewish critics, and follows Berne's agreement last Wednesday to set up a humanitarian fund for Holocaust survivors.
Bergier told Swiss Television on Saturday that research into Switzerland's actions during World War Two would give the country a chance to come to grips with its past.
"I see the entire matter as an opportunity for Switzerland to again find itself and solve its identity problems," Bergier said.

The commission is already under pressure to deliver two fast reports demanded by the cabinet in the next few months, on Swiss central bank purchases of Nazi gold and on Berne's wartime policy of rejecting Jewish refugees.
It is also likely to tackle the question of how insurance companies dealt with Jewish policy holders.
On Sunday the weekly paper Sonntags Zeitung said Swiss life insurers collaborated with the Nazis and agreed in 1944 not to pay out on German Jews' insurance policies from their Swiss offices.
The Bergier commission's two priority reports will help decide whether the Swiss government pays into the Holocaust memorial fund launched last week with money from Swiss banks.
Berne hopes to ward off a right-wing backlash against putting taxpayers' money into the fund by using the reports to back up arguments that it is morally obliged to pay for wartime policy mistakes.
Blocher's statements on Saturday, in front of 1,000 cheering people, showed that many Swiss are tired and annoyed by the harsh criticism that has been levelled against them.

Switzerland should stand up against "the excessive accusations from domestic and foreign circles and demands for money," Blocher said, adding it would be an act of betrayal for companies, banks or the federal government to pay or apologise for Switzerland's economic policy during the war.

After completing the two priority reports, Bergier's researchers can begin the broader task of charting the size and flow of assets sent to the neutral banking nation for wartime safety, for sale or for transfer to the wider world.

"This is a huge task...The situation is such that we do not even know exactly what areas (of this history) we don't know about," Swiss historian and commission member Jakob Tanner told a historical seminar last week.

Berne set up the panel after months of accusations led by the World Jewish Congress (WJC) that Swiss banks hoarded accounts left by victims of Nazi genocide and that the country profited as a banking and business centre for Nazi Germany.

It is separate from a commission chaired by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker set up last May by Swiss banks and the WJC to sweep Swiss bank records for accounts left by victims of Nazi genocide.
Both groups share one unprecedented privilege -- the legal power to lift secrecy rules on historical bank records. Volcker and Bergier hope to share their resources and findings.
